title: 1 Kings 13:1–10
context: After the kingdom divides, Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan and appoints his own priests and feast (12:28–33). As he stands at the Bethel altar, an unnamed man of God from Judah cries out against it, naming Josiah, a future king of David's line who will defile it. The altar splits, Jeroboam's outstretched hand withers, and is restored at the prophet's prayer. The man of God refuses the king's hospitality, because the LORD has told him not to eat, drink, or return the way he came.

verses.text: Behold, a man of God came out of Judah by the LORD’s word to Bethel; and Jeroboam was standing by the altar to burn incense.
verses.arminianNotes: A man of God comes from Judah "by the LORD's word" while Jeroboam burns incense at Bethel. Arminian readers note that God confronts Jeroboam's false worship directly, giving the king a real opportunity to turn back.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God sends his word into the heart of Jeroboam's rival worship. The king's altar at Bethel, built to keep Israel from Jerusalem (12:28), is challenged by a prophet from Judah.

verses.text: He cried against the altar by the LORD’s word, and said, “Altar! Altar! The LORD says: ‘Behold, a son will be born to David’s house, Josiah by name. On you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places who burn incense on you, and they will burn men’s bones on you.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The prophecy names Josiah, born to David's house, who will burn the bones of the priests on this altar. Arminian readers note the striking specificity, a warning given long beforehand that Jeroboam's system will not last.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 23:15–16 records the fulfillment "according to the LORD's word which the man of God proclaimed." God's word governs history across generations and comes to pass exactly.

verses.text: He gave a sign the same day, saying, “This is the sign which the LORD has spoken: Behold, the altar will be split apart, and the ashes that are on it will be poured out.”
verses.arminianNotes: The man of God gives a sign: the altar will split and its ashes pour out. Arminian readers see God graciously confirming his word, giving Jeroboam visible evidence that should move him to repent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the immediate sign authenticates the distant prophecy. God's word is shown to be true now, so that its later fulfillment through Josiah can be trusted.

verses.text: When the king heard the saying of the man of God, which he cried against the altar in Bethel, Jeroboam put out his hand from the altar, saying, “Seize him!” His hand, which he put out against him, dried up, so that he could not draw it back again to himself.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeroboam stretches out his hand to seize the prophet, and it dries up. Arminian readers see the king's choice to resist God met with immediate judgment, a vivid warning against opposing God's messenger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God protecting his servant and humbling the king. The hand raised against the prophet becomes powerless, a picture of how human power fails when set against God's word.

verses.text: The altar was also split apart, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign which the man of God had given by the LORD’s word.
verses.arminianNotes: The altar splits and the ashes pour out, "according to the sign." Arminian readers note that God's word proves true at once, removing any excuse for Jeroboam to dismiss the warning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the precise fulfillment as a testimony to God's faithfulness to his word. The sign shows that the worship Jeroboam devised stands under God's judgment.

verses.text: The king answered the man of God, “Now intercede for the favor of the LORD your God, and pray for me, that my hand may be restored to me.” The man of God interceded with the LORD, and the king’s hand was restored to him, and became as it was before.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeroboam asks the man of God to pray, and his hand is restored. Arminian readers see God's mercy offered even to a rebellious king, an opening to repentance that Jeroboam will not take (13:33).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God shows kindness to Jeroboam through the prophet's intercession. The king seeks relief from judgment but not a change of heart, as verse 33 makes plain.

verses.text: The king said to the man of God, “Come home with me and refresh yourself, and I will give you a reward.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king invites the man of God home for refreshment and a reward. Arminian readers note the subtle temptation: hospitality and reward could blur the prophet's witness and seem to endorse Bethel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jeroboam may hope to win the prophet's favor and soften the judgment. The offer tests whether God's messenger will remain faithful to his commission.

verses.text: The man of God said to the king, “Even if you gave me half of your house, I would not go in with you, neither would I eat bread nor drink water in this place;
verses.arminianNotes: "Even if you gave me half of your house, I would not go in with you." Arminian readers admire the prophet's firm, freely chosen obedience, refusing even great reward to stay true to God's word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the prophet's resolve in the face of royal favor. Faithfulness to God's word outweighs every earthly reward, a contrast with what will happen later in the chapter.

verses.text: for so was it commanded me by the LORD’s word, saying, ‘You shall eat no bread, drink no water, and don’t return by the way that you came.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The command was to eat no bread, drink no water, and not return the same way. Arminian readers note that the command's purpose is to show that Bethel stands under judgment; fellowship there would compromise the message.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the command embodies the message: no table fellowship with a place under God's curse. The prophet's conduct is meant to proclaim the same word his lips proclaim.

verses.text: So he went another way, and didn’t return by the way that he came to Bethel.
verses.arminianNotes: He goes home another way. Arminian readers see obedience completed so far, while the following episode will test whether it endures under a more subtle temptation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the prophet has obeyed the letter of his command to this point. The next scene will show that obedience must persevere even when a seemingly authoritative voice says otherwise.
